readerTitle: A second store on borrowed money: four calls in a row
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (철물·원예 매장 2호점 대출) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 회사 안의 팀 맥락은 Watch out 카드와 softwareNote에서 다룸
insight: 대출 결정은 '계획대로 되면 얼마 버나'가 아니라 '나쁜 해에도 상환하고 버틸 현금이 남나'로 판단한다.
misconception: 계획상 이익이 대출 상환액보다 크면 빌려서 키우는 게 안전하다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (레버리지, 유동성, 위험과 수익, 복리 성장)

cards.title: The bank says yes. Now the hard part starts.
body: You own a busy hardware and garden store. A shop across town is empty, and the bank will lend you $300,000 to open a second one.
The plan looks great. Over the next four decisions, you'll find out whether the plan survives a bad year.

image.label: A store owner holding a key in front of an empty shopfront
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 철물·원예 매장 주인이 빈 상가 앞에서 열쇠를 들고 서 있고, 한 손에는 은행 서류. 유리창에 'For lease' 종이. 실제 은행·브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your numbers today.
body: The plan says store 2 would sell about $1,000,000 a year and earn **$90,000** once running. The loan: up to $300,000 at 8%, repaid over five years.

breakdown.label: Left each year
breakdown.detail: After all costs and your own pay

cards.title: Borrow now or save up?
body: The landlord wants an answer this month. What do you do?

options.text: Wait about 15 months, save the rest, and pay cash
options.feedback: No payments and no lender. But you give up more than $100,000 of planned profit, and the site may go to someone else.

options.text: Borrow and sign this week. Store 2 should earn more than the payments
options.feedback: That's true only if the plan comes true. The payments are fixed. The sales aren't.

options.text: Borrow, but first check whether you could make the payments in a bad year
options.feedback: You keep the chance to grow now, and you learn how much risk the loan really adds before you sign.

cards.title: A bad year, on paper.
body: You imagine a slow year. Both stores share one town, so both slip. Store 2 sells 25% below plan, and its profit disappears.
On a full $300,000 loan, you'd be **$13,000 short**. You can survive that only if cash covers the gap.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company, the fixed payment is often a team. Hiring ahead of revenue works like a loan against future sales. Run the same test: if new revenue lands 25% below plan, how many months of cash are left?

cards.title: How much of your own cash goes in?
body: You have $150,000. Store 2 costs $300,000. In each option, the bad-year result is store 1's $60,000 minus the yearly payments.

options.text: Borrow all $300,000 and keep all your cash. Payments: $73,000 a year
options.feedback: The biggest cushion, easily covering a $13,000 gap. But you pay 8% on $100,000 more than you need, about $8,000 in the first year.

options.text: Put in all $150,000 and borrow $150,000. Payments: $36,500
options.feedback: A bad year still leaves $23,500, but you have no cash at all. One broken delivery van or slow month and you're calling the bank.

options.text: Put in $100,000, borrow $200,000 and keep $50,000. Payments: $48,700
options.feedback: A bad year still leaves about $11,300, and $50,000 sits ready for surprises. Smaller payments than A, and the cushion B lacks.

cards.title: A discount you can't quite afford.
body: Say you chose C. Eight months in, store 2 is selling 25% below plan. Store 1 is fine.
A supplier offers 15% off if you buy $80,000 of next season's stock now. The bank will lend it short term.

image.label: A stockroom stacked high with boxes and a price tag reading 15% off
image.brief: 매장 창고에 상자가 천장까지 쌓여 있고 '15% off' 가격표가 붙어 있음. 한쪽에 '$50,000 cash'라고 적힌 작은 금고. 상자 무게에 눌린 느낌. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

options.text: Borrow $80,000 and take the full deal. You save $12,000
options.feedback: A second payment arrives while store 2 is weak, and your money sits in boxes that may sell slowly. A good price on stock you can't sell is not a saving.

options.text: Buy only store 1's half, $40,000, with the short-term loan. You save $6,000
options.feedback: Store 1's stock will sell, so the risk is smaller. But you still add debt before you know if store 2 will recover.

options.text: Decline, keep the $50,000 cash, and fix store 2's costs first
options.feedback: You give up $12,000 of discount. You keep your cushion in cash while the weakest part of the plan is still unproven.

cards.title: The bank wants to lend you more.
body: Say you kept your cash. You trimmed store 2's hours and stock, and by month 20 it's running close to plan.
The bank is pleased. It offers another $300,000 for a third store.

options.text: Sign now, while the bank is willing
options.feedback: Two loans, one store barely proven and a $50,000 cushion. A bad year now would hit three stores' payments at once.

options.text: Stop growing and pay off the first loan early
options.feedback: The safest path, but you give up the return you took the risk for. Standing still has a cost too.

options.text: Wait until store 2 has a full year near plan and cash is rebuilt, then rerun the bad-year test
options.feedback: You grow again, on proof instead of hope, with a cushion sized for the bigger debt.

cards.title: The test is only as good as its guesses.
body: Your bad year assumed both stores fell together, because they share one town. That was the right instinct. Real bad years rarely hit just one part of a business.
Halving profit is still a guess. A worse year, or a rate that rises on a variable loan, can break a plan that passed the test.
The same logic applies inside larger companies. A team that hires ahead of next year's budget takes on a fixed cost against uncertain revenue.

image.label: Two storefronts under one storm cloud
image.brief: 같은 동네에 있는 매장 두 곳 위에 먹구름 하나가 함께 떠 있음. 두 매장 모두 손님이 줄어든 분위기. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Borrow for growth you could survive missing.
body: Each decision you made was one idea from this unit:
list: **Borrow now or wait → Leverage:** debt speeds growth, but the payments stay fixed while sales move.
**How much cash to keep → Liquid vs illiquid:** cash on hand turns a bad year into a setback, not a crisis.
**The stock deal → Risk and return:** a $12,000 discount wasn't worth more debt and stock that sells slowly.
**The third store → Compound growth:** growth only compounds if you survive long enough to keep growing.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your biggest fixed commitment. Cut next year's revenue by a quarter and check whether you can still pay it.
